## Rivers

Rivers are among the oldest storytellers on Earth. Long before people wrote anything down, rivers were carving their histories into rock, cutting canyons, and building floodplains grain by grain. Each bend and bank is a record of centuries of patient work, where water, gravity and time have shaped the land.

A river begins humbly, as a spring bubbling from the ground, a melting glacier, or rain gathering on a hillside. Small streams join and grow, and over hundreds or thousands of miles they become the Amazon, the Nile or the Mississippi. Along the way a river collects sediment, nutrients and life, and carries them from mountains to the sea. It is a conveyor belt that feeds deltas, builds wetlands, and keeps coastlines in balance.

For people, rivers have always meant survival. The first great civilizations grew along the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus, the Yellow River and the Nile. Rivers gave those societies water to drink, fertile soil for crops, and highways for trade. Cities rose where rivers could be crossed or where they met the ocean. Even today, much of the world's population lives within reach of a river, and many economies still depend on their flow.

Rivers are also living ecosystems. Salmon swim upstream against strong currents to spawn where they were born. Otters, herons, dragonflies and countless microorganisms rely on clean, moving water. Healthy riverbanks filter pollution, slow floods and give shelter to wildlife.

Yet rivers are fragile. Dams, pollution, overuse and climate change threaten many of them. Some no longer reach the sea at all. Protecting rivers means protecting ourselves, since their health reflects the health of the land they drain.

To stand beside a river is to watch time in motion: always leaving and always arriving, never quite the same water twice.
